books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

stimulus.text:
"We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us. Too long has the publick been deceived by misrepresentations, in things which concern us dearly." — Freedom’s Journal, first issue, March 16, 1827.

The paper was founded in New York City by John Brown Russwurm and Samuel Cornish, the first newspaper owned and run by Black Americans.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Freedom's Journal, first issue, March 16, 1827. Wording checked against the Library of Congress exhibition text and the Gilder Lehrman transcription of “To Our Patrons.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Freedom's Journal (1827)
stem: Why would a Black-owned newspaper matter to the antislavery cause in the 1820s?

options.text: It let white editors explain slavery to Black readers
options.misconception: The point is Black editors speaking, not white editors explaining.

options.text: It gave Black writers a platform to answer attacks and organize readers
It proved that most white Americans in the North already opposed slavery
options.misconception: Abolitionism was a minority view among Northern whites.

options.text: It ended the domestic slave trade within a year
options.misconception: The trade grew for decades after 1827.

rationales.A: The Journal reversed the usual direction. Black editors spoke; white readers listened.
rationales.B: The paper answered attacks on Black people and carried debate, news, and notices to readers in many states.
rationales.C: Most Northern whites did not oppose slavery in the 1820s. The paper argued against a majority, it did not reflect one.
rationales.D: The domestic slave trade kept growing long after 1827. No newspaper ended it in a year.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the paper changed. Before 1827, Black voices rarely appeared in print except when accused of crimes.
2. Ask what it carried. News, debates, school and job notices, and answers to attacks on Black people.
3. Name the power. A press of their own let Black writers argue and organize.
Background: The paper reached readers in eleven states and in Haiti, Europe, and Canada.
Remember: a newspaper is not only news; it is a meeting place in print.
